dimensions.description: Needs clear goals, expectations, and success criteria — including quality bar and definition of done — established before starting work
Prefers written documentation as the primary source of truth for alignment
Learns from existing examples, code, tickets, or past work rather than descriptions
Prefers live conversation over written documentation for staying aligned
Learns how a collaboration or system works by trying something real rather than reading about it first
Comfortable working with incomplete information or undefined constraints
Needs clear definition of who owns which decisions and responsibilities
Prefers live visibility into progress, blockers, and state rather than periodic summaries
Needs to understand team norms, roles, and interpersonal context — whether to integrate into a new team or to make well-informed decisions about situations involving multiple people
Needs explicit shared agreement before acting — uncomfortable with unverified assumptions
Expects risks, gaps, and problems to be surfaced early and openly rather than held back
Prefers alignment and updates at predictable, structured moments rather than continuously
Values protecting uninterrupted work time; sensitive to unnecessary context switching
Prefers addressing misalignment or blockers as soon as they appear rather than waiting
Prefers fixed delivery cycles with dedicated planning, review, and reflection moments
Prefers continuous work pulled from a prioritized backlog without fixed cycles or waiting
Prefers clarifying full scope, dependencies, and milestones before beginning execution
Prefers refining the plan progressively as work progresses and more is learned
Prefers grounding plans in small experiments or observable signals before committing to a direction
Expects to be involved in decisions that affect their work before those decisions are finalized
Expects changes to be batched into planning points rather than introduced mid-flow
Expects new work to require an explicit trade-off against existing commitments rather than being added on top
Values maintaining a sustainable workload and resisting scope or pace inflation
Expects trade-offs, alternatives considered, and what is being given up to be made explicit
Comfortable accepting scope or plan changes without requiring extensive process or justification
Considers work done when the core problem is solved reliably; follow-up items should not always be a gate
Needs a peer review or external check before trusting a handoff or considering work complete
Prefers assessing severity and actual impact before reacting; values proportionate responses over immediate alarm

Prefers resolving problems independently before involving others; when in a leading role, encourages direct resolution between parties first before intervening — avoids creating unnecessary noise or dependency
Prioritizes understanding why a problem happened alongside fixing it, to prevent recurrence
Protects the quality bar even under deadline pressure; treats some quality risks as non-negotiable
Prioritizes owning and fixing a problem over explaining or questioning it; repair-first orientation
Validates whether a concern reflects a real gap before accepting it; does not treat every finding as a problem by default
When giving feedback, prioritizes accuracy and substance over delivery style; believes valid concerns should not be dismissed due to discomfort
When giving feedback, believes delivery style is essential to effectiveness; adjusts how feedback is given so the other person can actually use it
When receiving feedback, extracts useful signal even from poor delivery; does not let style get in the way of hearing the concern
When receiving feedback, needs delivery to be appropriate before being able to process the concern; style affects ability to engage
Prefers to explicitly agree on shared norms for how concerns and feedback are exchanged, not just resolve the immediate instance
Prefers to raise concerns privately first; treats public discussion of problems as a last resort
Needs public feedback to be handled respectfully and without embarrassment; dignity is a precondition for engagement
Needs a private follow-up conversation after public feedback exchanges; repair happens separately from the public discussion
Expects to manage their own work tempo without regular monitoring; frequent purposeless check-ins feel like distrust
Expects to decide HOW to execute work they own; detailed direction within owned scope feels like a lack of trust in their judgment
Accepts oversight when it comes from a place of support; rejects oversight that feels driven by anxiety, distrust, or a need to approve every step
Needs access to guidance or decision help when blocked; unavailable support on important decisions feels like abandonment
Needs ongoing calibrating signals and encouragement, not just feedback when something goes wrong
When blocked or unsure, prefers a concrete decision or recommendation over collaborative exploration; wants to be unblocked, not facilitated
Needs to be able to ask for support without it being interpreted as a lack of competence; psychological safety to seek help is part of healthy ownership
Needs collaborative interactions to produce a concrete, visible outcome — a decision, next step, or documented result; time without tangible output is hard to justify
Values regular synchronous contact for team cohesion and human connection beyond task-based interaction; familiarity and rhythm matter independently of output
Needs urgency communicated calmly and factually; does not want stress, anxiety, or pressure to be performed — clarity over dramatisation
Galvanized by high-pressure, consequence-laden, or accountability-based urgency communication; responds to stress-driven framing
Motivated by positive, encouraging, and purpose-driven framing; responds to excitement and support rather than pressure or consequences
Self-motivated and does not need external motivational input; finds speeches or pep talks before deadlines distracting rather than helpful
Addresses interpersonal friction directly with the person involved, even when uncomfortable; willing to name patterns that bother them
Genuinely absorbs uncomfortable communication styles without needing to address them; personal discomfort is not sufficient reason to escalate
Uses team impact rather than personal discomfort as the threshold for action; subordinates own comfort to team function
Avoids direct confrontation of uncomfortable patterns; needs distance and processing time before deciding whether to act
Processes interpersonal friction by naming it to a trusted third party rather than raising it directly with the person involved
Believes interpersonal tension needs time and space to settle before a direct conversation can be productive; engaging while tension is still active tends to produce reactions rather than resolution
Readily involves higher authority when a problem exceeds what the direct parties can resolve; treats escalation as a legitimate and timely tool rather than a last resort
In difficult conversations, prioritizes both perspectives being genuinely heard over reaching a concrete outcome or agreement; needs acknowledgment before being able to move on

In difficult conversations, expects both parties to acknowledge their part rather than one person identifying the problem and the other owning the fix — for example, if a deadline was missed, both the person who missed it and the person who set unclear expectations should own something

Views structured facilitation as a legitimate tool for resolving conflict — whether as a participant open to third-party help, or as a leader actively stepping in to bring conflicting parties together in a structured way

Believes conflict resolves more reliably when a team builds deliberate habits — such as retrospectives that include interpersonal health, explicit norms for raising concerns, or regular check-ins where naming tension is normalized — rather than relying on ad-hoc intervention after something breaks
Motivated primarily by the quality and difficulty of the work itself; finds genuine satisfaction in building things well and solving hard problems, independent of external recognition or purpose
Needs to understand why work matters and how it connects to a meaningful outcome; motivation drops significantly when work feels disconnected from purpose or when the reason behind a task is unclear
Motivated primarily by being given real ownership and the freedom to make decisions; without genuine trust and responsibility, work loses its meaning
Motivated primarily by the people, team, and shared experience of building something together; relationships matter more as a source of drive than the work itself
Values being seen and acknowledged during difficult or pressured periods more than routine praise; recognition when things are hard feels more meaningful than being praised when things are easy
Finds a workday worthwhile when understanding of the problem, system, or people has genuinely improved; values insight and better mental models as an end in themselves, even without visible output
Believes process, planning, and delivery reliability are important enough to examine as a team; considers operational execution the core topic for retrospectives
Believes technical quality, incidents, and maintainability deserve regular team reflection; considers soundness as important as delivery speed
Believes collaboration patterns and communication habits are worth examining as a team, even when they feel less urgent than delivery; expects friction here to eventually show up in the work
Believes team safety, pressure, and how people are treated are foundational reflection topics; thinks problems hidden by unsafe culture are the hardest to fix later
